summary:
The Northern Mariana Islands is a US commonwealth and stands under the national framework of the United States for travel documents, immigration and airport screening. United States passports and entry documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X marker option was eliminated by the January 2025 executive order, so a trans visitor travelling on United States documents presents a gender marker that may not match presentation at the port of entry.

Screening at the airport follows federal procedure, and the order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in the territory, so access to such care during a visit cannot be assumed. In February 2025 the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports.

There is no criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct or of gender expression under Commonwealth law. Commonwealth Public Law 22-32, signed in January 2023, amends the Commonwealth Code to set criteria for enhanced sentencing in hate-motivated crimes, and the statute covers offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity; this is the principal local protection a visitor would be able to invoke after an identity-based assault, though the sources do not document how it has been applied.

Legal gender recognition exists in the territory, but only on condition that the applicant has undergone the specified medical process. A visitor relying on locally issued documents rather than a United States passport should expect that medical requirement to apply.

There is no comprehensive local nondiscrimination ordinance covering gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations. Beyond federal law, protection extends only to government employees, leaving private-sector and service-access discrimination to be pursued through federal EEOC recourse.
tangentialFactors:
The Movement Advancement Project equality profile for the Northern Mariana Islands, dated 27 September 2026, scores sexual orientation policy at 3.5 out of 22 (Low) and gender identity policy at minus 2 out of 25 (Negative), for an overall score of 1.5 out of 47 (Low). The negative gender identity score places the territory below most United States jurisdictions on trans-specific policy.

Marriage recognition scores a full point, in place since 2015, when Obergefell v. Hodges reached the territory by operation of the federal constitution; the first same-sex marriage on Saipan was officiated on 27 July 2015. Adoption by same-sex couples has been available since 2015 as well. The gap between full marriage recognition and absent gender-identity coverage is the defining feature of the local regime.

Social climate indicators are modest: the territory's first Gay Pride event was held at the GIG Discotheque in Garapan with roughly 60 people attending, and the organiser, Sharmaine Casquero, described it as a success. Public visibility remains limited rather than suppressed.
localsOnly:
Commonwealth Public Law 22-32, signed in January 2023, provides criteria for enhanced sentencing of defendants convicted of hate-motivated crimes and covers offences motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity. Residents can rely on it as a sentencing enhancement rather than as a standalone offence.

Nondiscrimination protection for residents is confined to government employees under local law; private employment and commercial services fall back on federal EEOC process. There is no comprehensive Commonwealth statute on gender identity or sexual orientation in housing, public accommodations or credit.

Legal gender change is available under Commonwealth law provided the applicant has undergone the specified medical process. Same-sex couples may marry and adopt, both in place since 2015.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not document any prosecution or enhanced sentence under Commonwealth Public Law 22-32, so its practical effect for a victim of an anti-trans assault is unresolved.

Whether the January 2025 federal marker restrictions govern documents issued by the Commonwealth itself, as distinct from United States passports, is not addressed in the inventory and remains unresolved.

No sourced material covers restroom or facility access, school policy, local healthcare-facility intake practice, or police conduct toward trans detainees in the territory. The Movement Advancement Project scores are dated 27 September 2026 and may not reflect later legislative action. The Pride attendance figure and the organiser's assessment come from a single local report.
